title: The MC146818 real-time clock, its registers
covers: The registers of the MC146818 real-time clock: the time, calendar and alarm bytes, the control and status registers and the general purpose RAM

A read of the seconds location returns a value of the decimal range Table 3 lists.
A write to the seconds location sets it to a value of the decimal range Table 3 lists.
A write stores the byte with bit 7 cleared, with no range check in this case body.
The memory has 50 general purpose RAM bytes, 10 bytes of time, calendar and alarm data and four control and status bytes, all directly readable and writable except as listed.

rows.text: Register A at $0A holds UIP, DV2, DV1, DV0, RS3, RS2, RS1 and RS0 from bit 7 down to bit 0.
Every bit of Register A is read/write except UIP.
A read of Register A returns its bits; the UIP status flag may be monitored by the program.
UIP at 1 means an update cycle is in progress or about to begin; at 0 none is, or will be for at least 244 us (capture reads 'ps').
The time, calendar and alarm bytes are fully available to the program when UIP is zero, since they are not in transition.
UIP is a read-only bit.
Writing the SET bit of Register B to 1 inhibits any update cycle and then clears the UIP bit.
DV2, DV1 and DV0 let the program select various conditions of the 22-stage divider chain.
RS3, RS2, RS1 and RS0 select one of 15 taps on the 22-stage divider, or disable the divider output (capture of lines 981-983 damaged).
Writing register 0x0B with SET newly set clears the update-ended interrupt enable bit from the stored byte and refreshes the IRQ line; this body does not clear the UIP bit.
UIP reads 1 for 244 microseconds after the last update ended, so the window follows the update, and never while SET is 1.
A write stores the byte with bit 7 cleared; a DV value other than 0x20 logs a warning, and the rate comes from the low four bits.

rows.text: Register B at $0B holds SET, PIE, AIE, UIE, SQWE, DM, 24/12 and DSE from bit 7 down to bit 0.
Register B is a read/write register.
A read of Register B returns its bits.
With SET at 0 the update cycle functions normally, advancing the counts once per second.
Writing SET to 1 aborts any update cycle in progress so the program can initialize time and calendar without an update.
SET is a read/write bit.
PIE is a read/write bit which allows the periodic flag PF in Register C to cause the IRQ pin to be driven low.
A zero in PIE blocks IRQ from a periodic interrupt, but the periodic flag PF is still set at the periodic rate.
AIE set to 1 permits the alarm flag AF in Register C to assert IRQ (capture of lines 1015-1017 damaged).
An alarm inte[damaged] occurs for each second that the three time bytes [word lost] the three alarm bytes; a don't-care alarm code is binary 1IXXXXX (glyph doubtful).
With AIE at 0 the part does not initiate an IRQ signal (capture of lines 1020-1022 damaged).
The predicate of UIE is destroyed in the capture of lines 1023-1025; it reads as the update-ended flag (UF) bit in Register C, probably enabled to assert IRQ.
The SET bit going [word damaged in the capture, probably high] clears the UIE bit.
With SQWE at 1 a square-wave signal appears on the SQW pin (capture of lines 1028-1031 damaged).
With SQWE at 0 the SQW pin is held low; SQWE is a read/write bit.
DM tells whether updates use binary or BCD: a 1 in DM signifies binary data and a 0 specifies BCD.
DM is written by the program and may be read.
The 24/12 bit selects the 24-hour mode at 1 and the 12-hour mode at 0, and is a read/write bit.
DSE is a read/write bit that lets the program enable two special daylight savings updates.
With DSE at 1 the time jumps from 1:59:59 AM to 3:00:00 AM on the last Sunday in April, and back to 1:00:00 AM in October.
A program writes a 1 to PIE to receive periodic interrupts at the rate specified by RS3, RS2, RS1 and RS0 in Register A.
The square-wave frequency is the one specified by the rate selection bits RS3 to RS0 (capture of lines 1029-1030 damaged).
Writing register 0x0B with SET newly set clears the UIE bit from the stored byte and refreshes the IRQ line; this body does not cancel an update already scheduled.
The header marks the daylight savings adjustment as a TODO; time_tick increments the hour by one and wraps at 24.
The line that sets PF sits inside a test of PIE, and IRQ 8 is raised when the interrupt was acknowledged and any flag bit of 0x70 is set.
The line that sets PF sits inside a test of PIE, so PF is not set at the periodic rate when PIE is 0.
The alarm check that sets AF is called inside a test of AIE.
The line that sets UF sits inside a test of UIE.
No line of the write case for 0x0B drives a square-wave output.
No line of the write case for 0x0B holds a SQW pin low.
No line of the clock tick tests bit 0 of 0x0B or adds a daylight savings adjustment.
The select handler stores the low six bits of the byte as the selected register and bit 7 in cmos.nmi.
Reset leaves register 0x0B selected, since it selects 0x0A and then 0x0B before its two writes.

rows.text: Register C at $0C holds IRQF, PF, AF and UF from bit 7 down, then four cells the capture reads as zeros (glyphs damaged).
Register C is read only.
IRQF is set when one or more of PF=PIE=1, AF=AIE=1 and UF=UIE=1 holds: IRQF = PF*PIE + AF*AIE + UF*UIE (the capture writes 1 as I).
Any time IRQF is 1 the IRQ pin is driven low (the pin name is damaged in the capture).
All flag bits of Register C are cleared after the program reads it.
PF is a read-only bit.
PF is set to 1 when a particular edge is detected on the selected tap of the divider chain, independent of the state of PIE.
The RS3 to RS0 bits establish the periodic rate.
PF at 1 initiates an IRQ signal (the pin name is damaged in the capture) and sets IRQF when PIE is also 1.
PF is cleared by a software read of Register C.
A 1 in AF, the alarm interrupt flag, indicates that the current time has matched the alarm time.
AF at 1 causes the IRQ pin to go low and IRQF to be 1, when AIE is also 1 (the capture damages the pin name and the 1).
A read of Register C clears AF.
UF, the update-ended interrupt flag, is set after each update cycle.
When UIE is 1, UF at 1 causes IRQF to be 1 and asserts IRQ (the capture damages the pin name and the 1s).
UF is cleared by a Register C read.
The unused bits b3 to b0 are read as zeros (the line says Status Register 1, here Register C; O for zero in the capture).
The unused bits b3 to b0 cannot be written (the line says Status Register 1, here Register C).
The flag clear and the IRQ line update sit inside a branch taken only when side effects are not disabled.
The timer event activates IRQ 8 when a read of register 0x0C has set the acknowledged flag and any of bits 6 to 4 of it is stored.
The line that sets PF sits inside a test of bit 6 of register 0x0B, so PF is stored only when that bit is set.
A read of register 0x0C sets bits 7 and 6 when bit 6 of registers 0x0B and 0x0C are both set; the timer event activates IRQ 8 separately.
A read of register 0x0C sets bits 7 and 5 when bit 5 of registers 0x0B and 0x0C are both set; the timer event activates IRQ 8 separately.
The line that sets UF sits inside a test of bit 4 of register 0x0B, so UF is stored only when that bit is set.
A read of register 0x0C sets bits 7 and 4 when bit 4 of registers 0x0B and 0x0C are both set; the timer event activates IRQ 8 separately.

rows.text: The general purpose RAM bytes are not dedicated within the MC146818A (the byte count is damaged in the capture).
The general purpose RAM bytes can be used by the processor program.
The general purpose RAM bytes are fully available during the update cycle.
The RAM bytes serve the need for low-power CMOS battery-backed storage of data that must be retained when main power is removed (parts of the sentence are damaged).
The sentence goes on about extending the available RAM and a part the capture reads as MC148818AS; the capture is too damaged to say more.

A read of register 0x10 returns a byte built from the BIOS types of the floppy images, and 0x12 one built from the two hard disk images.
With imageDiskList[2] attached, reads of 0x19 and 0x1b to 0x23 return 47, its cylinders, heads, 0xFF, a heads-derived byte, or its sectors; with none attached they return 0.
Reads of registers 0x1a and 0x24 to 0x2c return the same kind of values built from the second hard disk image, or 0 with none attached.
Reads of registers 0x39 and 0x3a return 0.
A read of register 0x2F returns 0xFF when the PS/1 audio card is enabled.
Registers 0x32 and 0x37 read the century of the emulated clock year; a valid write of 19 or more to either sets the century of that year.
A write of register 0x0F stores the byte with bit 7 cleared.
